scope_note: examples/steer/ read in full (README.md, run.py, test.sh, harnesses.py, provenance.json, entries/*.json, units/*.json, policy/*.json, schemas/steer.schema.json), plus the harness code it calls (harness/policy/interface.py, harness/human-interaction/interface.py and store.py, harness/containment/interface.py and binding.json), examples/end-to-end/schemas/entry.schema.json and run.py, examples/run/harnesses.py, docs/consumption/unit-design.md, docs/litmus/questionnaire.json, docs/maturity/closures.md, docs/reference/ontology.md, docs/architecture/proposed/steer.json, kb/facts.jsonl, kb/target-facts.jsonl, kb/research/*.jsonl, PASS.md, STATUS.md, OWNER.md, state/briefs/context-75.md, state/briefs/example-review.md and kb/ceremonies/75-run-review.json (for the record shape and the boundary the row-75 brief carries forward). Nothing the author wrote about the example outside examples/steer/ was read. A repository-wide grep for the misquoted wording in R75STEER-001 incidentally printed two lines of state/plants-steer.json; that file was not opened, and every finding below was reached from the example and the records it cites. Files touched: kb/ceremonies/75-steer-review.json and docs/night/hidden/steer.sh only. Running the example, its gate and the hidden check rewrote examples/steer/out/, which is gitignored and regenerated by test.sh; the hidden check removes its own out/hid-* artefacts on exit.

h-03 the effect decision is identical in point, action, effect, rule and resource at all four doors, and each door ends the way its own steer declaration says: an approve completes with the effect fired, a 'none' fails with a deadline-exceeded refusal and no effect, a reject escalates at least once

h-04 every ledger record carries run id, correlation id, actor, delegation depth, entry kind and idempotency key, and every record kind the runner actually emits (six runs, including the revised one) is named in the README's receipt row. FAILS: policy-activated is emitted and not named

h-10 every id-attributed quote in the README (58 of them) is verbatim in the record carrying that id, across kb/facts.jsonl, kb/target-facts.jsonl, kb/reference-facts.jsonl, kb/research.jsonl and kb/research/*.jsonl. FAILS: F-b1-03

findings.evidence: The Ideal table's `policy` row attributes to `F-b1-03` the quote "Each interface names the standard that governs it. Where a standard exists, adopt it whole rather than creating our own framework." F-b1-03's text in kb/facts.jsonl (and in PASS.md:114, its source) is "2. **Each interface names the standard that governs it.** Where a standard exists, adopt it whole rather than modelling our own shape." `grep -rn 'creating our own framework'` over the repository returns this README line and nothing else, while the correct wording is quoted verbatim at eight other sites (kb/facts.jsonl, PASS.md, state/briefs/context-66.md, .claude/skills/build-evidence, cap-identity, cap-model-access, build-ceremony). The README's own opening rule (lines 10-15) is that every row is cited "with a verbatim quote, or it says proposed", and this is the ideal row for the `policy` litmus section - the row the area is scored against. Mechanically checked: of the 58 id-attributed quotes in this README, this is the only one that is not a substring of the record it names (docs/night/hidden/steer.sh h-10).
findings.fix: Replace the second citation with F-b1-03's verbatim text - "Where a standard exists, adopt it whole rather than modelling our own shape." - or drop it; the questionnaire quotes in the same cell already carry the row.

findings.location: examples/steer/run.py:668-681 (the expire branch of ask_and_decide, line 674); examples/steer/README.md:79 and 112
findings.evidence: `ask_and_decide` calls `parked = surface.expire(ask_id, now)` unguarded whenever `payload.steer.decision` is "none". The store refuses to sweep an ask that is still open (harness/human-interaction/store.py:302, `if now <= parked.ask['deadline_at']: raise Problem('document-invalid', ...)`), so any schema-valid declaration with `decision: "none"` and a `decision_delay_seconds` inside `gate.deadline_seconds` ends in an uncaught `interface.Problem` and a Python traceback on stderr: `python3 run.py --entry entries/schedule.json --decision none --delay 10` exits 1 with `interface.Problem: ask-steer-schedule-change-guard-1 is open until 2026-09-04T02:05:38Z`. The schema permits it (`decision_delay_seconds` is `integer, minimum 0`), and the only value the example ever runs is 400 against a 300-second deadline, so the visible check's `passed 90` covers one side of the pair. This contradicts README:112 ("A refusal that ends the unit | `application/problem+json` on stdout and a non-zero exit"), README:79's claim that `decision_delay_seconds` is read "against `gate.deadline_seconds`" as a two-sided differential, and F-b4-07 "Typed and machine-readable. Never parsed from prose" - a stack trace is neither. Every other refusal in this file goes through `problem()`/`render_problem()`.
findings.fix: Wrap the expire call the way the decide call below it is wrapped: catch `hi.Problem`, render it through `render_problem`, record it as a refusal and return a typed outcome - the deadline is the store's to enforce, not the runner's to assume. Then add the missing half of the differential to test.sh: the same door at a delay inside the deadline, asserted to produce a typed problem and no ask.expired event.

findings.evidence: The last row of section 3's call table, "unified framework", repeats the row directly above it (line 63, "the unit behind all four | `intent.workflow_ref` -> `units/steer-checkout-coupon-fix.json` | ... | nothing | one declaration, four doors") with every term renamed: "a single task structure, submission wrapper, authorization junction, and rule framework" for the "one unit declaration, one envelope shape, one decision point, one rule set" that the four door rows above already carry. Its reason is circular - "all four doors exercise one task specification" in the second column is answered by "`units/steer-checkout-coupon-fix.json` is the single specification" in the third. Two further problems: the table's first column is the door, and "unified framework" is not a door; and the four renamed terms appear nowhere else in the repository (`grep -rn 'submission wrapper|authorization junction|rule framework|task structure'` returns only this line), which is vocabulary drift away from docs/reference/ontology.md, whose terms the context brief requires (task specification, envelope, decision point, rule set).
findings.fix: Delete the row. Line 63 already states the property, in the ontology's words, and the measured sentence at lines 66-70 is what proves it.

findings.evidence: Steps 2 to 11 are printed without `--ledger`, so they all share the default ledger name `out/run.jsonl` and therefore the parked-ask store `out/asks/run/<correlation_id>`. Five of them re-enter through the same envelope: steps 2, 6, 7, 8 and 10 all use `entries/human.json`, and 4 and 11 both use `entries/schedule.json`. Because the store is durable and the ask id is derived from `entry_id` alone (`ask_id = f"ask-{env['entry_id']}-{suffix}"`, run.py:639), running the table in the order it is numbered gives step 2 the run it advertises and then refuses steps 6, 7, 10 and 11 at 409: `{"type": "urn:agentic:problem:idempotency-conflict", "detail": "ask ask-steer-human-coupon-fix-1 is already parked", "status": 409}` - reproduced from a clean `out/`, and asserted by docs/night/hidden/steer.sh h-13. None of those rows' "What it shows" column is a 409. test.sh does not hit this because every one of its runs is given a distinct `--ledger` basename; the note at lines 148-150 states the durability property but the commands under it are the ones that break on it. Step 12 compounds it: it verifies `out/human.jsonl`, which no step in the table writes - only test.sh does.
findings.fix: Print each step with the `--ledger out/<step>.jsonl` that test.sh already gives it, so the table is copy-pasteable in order, and point step 12 at a ledger a listed step wrote.

findings.evidence: All four entries declare `correlation.depth` (0, 0, 0, 1), which the shared entry schema makes optional, and README:62 sells it as part of what distinguishes the external door: "`agent:partner-sre-bot`, three hops, `parent_correlation_id`, `depth: 1`". Nothing reads it: `grep -n 'correlation\"\]\[\"depth' run.py` has no hit, and the depth every rule and every record uses is `len(env['actor']['delegation_chain'])`, computed at run.py:145 and 235. The differential the area's own rule prescribes confirms it: the external door run with `correlation.depth` set to 99 and with the member deleted produces the same status, disposition, effect_fired, refusal types and the same nine (point, action, effect, rule) decision rows - the only differences are the clock and the freshly minted unit ids. It is not in the carried-and-not-consumed table either, which does write up its neighbour `correlation.parent_correlation_id` and the derived `context.delegation_depth`. `envelope_version` is inert in the same way and is likewise unlisted, though it is fixed by the shared schema, as `budget.on_exceed` is - and that one is written up.
findings.fix: Either add a row to the carried-and-not-consumed table for `correlation.depth` (and `envelope_version`) with its research query - the natural one is whether a caller-declared depth should bound anything the platform does not derive from the chain itself - or drop the member from the entries and stop advertising it at line 62.

findings.evidence: provenance.json's measured list ends "...every record of the longest run carries the run id, correlation id, actor, delegation depth, entry kind and idempotency key across sixteen record kinds". The run test.sh's receipt check actually reads, out/external.jsonl, carries 13 distinct kinds; no ledger any run of this example writes carries more than 14 (out/escok.jsonl); 19 distinct kinds exist across all forty runs. Sixteen is the length of the README:111 enumeration, not a number read out of any artefact - the same shape as R75RUN-004. That enumeration is itself short by one: `policy-activated` is emitted by run.py:667 on every `--revise-policy` run and is named in neither the README row nor the test's receipt assertion, so the record kind that carries the area's central claim - a rule set starting to serve while the unit is parked - is the one kind nothing enumerates.
findings.fix: Count the kinds out of the ledger the sentence describes and write that number, or drop the count; and add `policy-activated` to the README receipt row and to test.sh's receipt assertion, run against a ledger that has one (out/revise.jsonl).

findings.evidence: The extension-points row "A different enforcement point" claims two things - "call `admit` at a new point and register its declared shape" and "an unregistered point is refused rather than defaulted to allow" - and names `test.sh` section 7 as the differential that proves them. Section 7 does neither: it makes the engine unreachable at each of the five points that policy/points.json already registers, which proves fail-closed and nothing about registration. No run in the example registers a sixth point, and none asks a decision at an unregistered one, although the mechanism exists on the interface the example imports (harness/policy/interface.py:281-286 raises `decision-point-unregistered` 422, "an unregistered point is a conformance failure, not a default-allow"). The same row's `journal.declared_subset` is carried into every report (run.py:308) and asserted by no check. Neither claim appears under provenance.claimed, so an unmeasured property is sitting in the measured column of the extension-points table.
findings.fix: Add one differential: register a sixth point through the interface and take a decision at it, and take a decision at a name that was never registered, asserting 422 and that no work ran. Or move the sentence into provenance.claimed and cite the harness's own gate as where it is proved.

findings.evidence: `report["decisions_at_effect"]` is a literal assigned by whichever branch of `fire_effect` ran - 1 under `--carry-decision`, 2 otherwise - and the breakage check at test.sh:194 asserts that literal ("2 to 1"), as does provenance.json's measured entry for the breakage. The number is true today (out/human.json carries two dispatch.tool_call rows and out/carry.json one) but it is read out of a constant the runner wrote about itself, not out of the decision rows that carry the fact; a gutted `fire_effect` that decided nothing and still set the field to 2 would pass. It is also wrong as a general count: the external door takes two dispatch.tool_call decisions across two attempts and never sets the field at all.
findings.fix: Count `[r for r in report['decisions'] if r['decision_point'] == 'dispatch.tool_call']` in the check instead of reading the field, as docs/night/hidden/steer.sh h-06 does; the field can stay as a convenience once nothing decides on it.

findings.evidence: "the effect decision is byte-identical at every one of them - same point, same action, same effect, same rule, same resource (`test.sh` section 1)". The check that section names (out/same-decision.log) compares exactly those five members and nothing else, and the decisions are not byte-identical: the four rows carry four different `input_digest` values (sha256:ff37967f..., 1207a33d..., 92a79059..., 6614a2fe...) and four different dispatch ids, because the context half of the input carries the run id, the correlation id and the entry kind, which is the property the very next sentence relies on. provenance.json states it correctly ("identical in point, action, effect, rule and resource"); the README overstates it by one adjective in the sentence that introduces the area's headline measurement.
findings.fix: Say "identical in point, action, effect, rule and resource", as provenance.json already does.

findings.evidence: The check backing the README's opening claim that "Nothing here names a product or a policy language outside the adapters and standards tables" is a single `grep -qiE "\bopa\b|rego|cedar|firecracker|openai|anthropic|langfuse|vendor" out/human.log` - one of the roughly forty logs the run writes, and none of the source files. A product name in run.py's comments, in a policy bundle's `detail`, in a unit declaration or in any of the other doors' output would pass. (The property does hold today: a grep over every .py, .sh and .json in the directory returns only the line of test.sh that names them in order to forbid them, and the README names them only inside the standards table.)
findings.fix: Scan the sources and every log rather than one log, skipping the line that does the scanning - docs/night/hidden/steer.sh h-11 is one way to write it.

plants_note: Two defects were planted. R75STEER-001 is confirmed by evidence, and is the same shape as the run area's first plant: a single-site quote that exists nowhere else in the repository, attributed to an id whose real text is quoted correctly at eight other sites, sitting in the ideal row the area is scored against. R75STEER-003 is nominated as the second on the shape the row-75 boundary describes: a single-site table row that duplicates the cited row above it with every term renamed and a circular reason, whose four renamed terms ("task structure", "submission wrapper", "authorization junction", "rule framework") return no other hit in the repository - the same shape as R75RUN-003. The other candidates are ranked below it because they repeat across sites or have siblings, which is authorial habit rather than an insertion: R75STEER-006's wrong count agrees between provenance.json and the README enumeration it was taken from (agreement between two files is not evidence, R75RUN-004); R75STEER-005's unread declaration has siblings in `envelope_version` and in the six members the carried-and-not-consumed table does write up, so the habit is one of writing up most of them and missing one; R75STEER-002 is a real crash but a plausible authorial gap, since the honest path never reaches it and no check varies the value; and R75STEER-004 follows from a default argument, not from an inserted sentence.
what_holds: The four doors are on disk, each one's kind matches its filename, all four validate against the reference example's published entry schema and all four payload.steer declarations against this example's schema with that example's own validator, and they converge on one task specification while carrying four actors, four run ids and four correlation ids.

Every id-attributed quote in the README except R75STEER-001 is verbatim in the record carrying that id, checked mechanically fragment by fragment across kb/facts.jsonl, kb/target-facts.jsonl, kb/reference-facts.jsonl, kb/research.jsonl and kb/research/*.jsonl; the six REF-anchored quotes are verbatim in the files they name; and the questionnaire's policy and concern-policy future_state texts are quoted exactly.
No product, engine or policy-language name appears in any source file of the area, or in the README outside the standards table and the adapters table.

The area's central property is measured rather than asserted: an allow is spent when its action fires or is abandoned. A rule set activated while the unit is parked flips the effect decision from allow to deny under a different bundle digest, the effect never fires, the unit ends failed, no effect-applied record is written, and the pre-pause decision still replays to allow against the version it was pinned to. Counted out of the decision rows rather than off the runner's own counter, this holds.

The deliberate breakage does what the design says it must: --carry-decision reuses the pre-pause allow, takes one effect decision instead of two, fires an effect the rules in force refuse, and writes decided_again false on the ledger.

Fail-closed holds at all five registered enforcement points: with the engine made unreachable at each in turn, the first undecided row is at that point, is typed adapter-unavailable, carries no rule id, ran no work, spent nothing, and the unit ends rejected or failed - undecided is a distinct record from a policy deny.

The gate on the visible check has both halves the row-75 boundary asks for: FLOOR=90 is declared, gated on with `[ "$PASS" -ge "$FLOOR" ]` as well as on `[ "$FAIL" -eq 0 ]`, and equals provenance.visible_checks_counted and the number printed. provenance.cites equals exactly the ids the files carry, in both directions, and it is the example's own check that says so.

Eleven of the twelve fields in the two 'where each field is read' tables are read at a point of decision and varied by a check that asserts two different records: workflow_ref (class and price), ceiling_micros, delegation_chain (the mandate that decides replace), tenant, retries_permitted, escalation.steps_permitted, escalation.authority, decisions_offered, effect.scope, intervention_policy.permitted, checkpoint_before_turn, surface and stall_first_turn all move a record when they move. The escalation is taken once or declined, never twice.

The published vocabulary is adopted rather than invented: all eight event types the human-interaction capability publishes are produced across the four doors and nothing outside them, the task state is a pure projection over the stream that the runner refuses to report outside the published set, and every disposition is one of the ontology's four.

The three gaps the area is honest about are measured rather than smoothed over: the 501 with no row in the shared closed registry comes back marked registry: absent, the four extension members the closed registry drops from a policy denial are named individually, and reconnect attaching to a unit the boundary had already destroyed is recorded in the report and written up as gap 3 with its research query.

docs/architecture/proposed/steer.json carries seven blueprint gaps, every row origin=proposed with a research query and no invented mechanism, and its statement is grounded in four observations that name the interface files they come from.
